required_revisions.text: Deposit the genome-wide start-codon analysis in full and cite it: custom tblastn scripts and parameter files, the gene presence/absence matrix, the per-gene per-genome start-codon call table, and the complete list of the 60,690 genome accessions used, in a public repository (Zenodo/GitHub) with a permanent DOI. Add a Data Availability statement and reference the DOI in Methods. This is the single condition on which acceptance most directly depends.

Deposit the primary experimental data: ARD1/3/5/6/10/12 Illumina reads to SRA under PRJNA1305691 with the Breseq VCFs as supplementary files; the pLM7UG1-like and pLMGC1 plasmid sequences to GenBank; and the full annotated sequences of the three pIMK3-rsbW-eGFP (ATG/ATA/ATT) and the pIMK3-plcB/lftR constructs as supplementary FASTA. List individual read and assembly accessions, not only the project accession.

Revise the title, Abstract and the Results header 'SC are under selection for stress response and virulence genes' to language reflecting association rather than selection (e.g. 'clade-associated variation'), and add a Discussion paragraph naming drift, founder effects, lineage-specific bias and hitchhiking as alternatives not excluded by phylogenetic co-occurrence. If any 'selection' claim is retained anywhere, it must be supported by dN/dS or fitness evidence.

Address the RsbV G111C/S confound explicitly. Either (a) include the isogenic native-locus rsbW-ATA/ATT allelic-exchange mutant assayed for colony morphology, motility and SigB-dependent transcripts, or (b) state clearly in Results (at Fig. 4D) and Discussion that the reporter assay tests start-codon identity only in a heterologous pIMK3/MQ140025 background, that RsbV substitutions co-vary with the start-codon changes in every relevant ARD, and that the causal contribution of each cannot be separated by the present data. Incorporate the graded LM/IM dose-response argument from the rebuttal into the manuscript text as positive evidence against a purely binary loss-of-function model.

Complete the statistical reporting: state the exact test for every panel in Figs. 1, 2, 4 and 5 (not only Fig. 2), define error bars as SD, SEM or CI in each legend, state the number of biological versus technical replicates for each panel, justify the paired t-test, report exact p-values for Fig. 2 in a supplementary table, and apply and report Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected q-values across the gene x strain comparisons.

Supply the missing computational provenance: version numbers and key parameters for Autocycler (and canu/flye/metaMDBG/unicycler), Prokka, BRIG, geneviewer, Mauve, tblastn (e-value, word size, coverage/identity cutoffs), Breseq, Parsnp2 and mlst; the exact filtering and counting logic for the >95% conservation and >5% flexibility thresholds; and a justification of the 5% threshold that incorporates the rebuttal's phylogenetic-clustering argument against sequencing/assembly artifact.

Add sequencing metadata: Nanopore read-length statistics (N50, mean), total bases and coverage depth for the MQ140025 assembly; and the Illumina platform, read length, insert size and per-isolate coverage depth for the ARD isolates.
Resolve the internal numerical inconsistency between the Abstract ('60,692 genomes') and Methods ('n=60,690'), and use the correct figure consistently throughout.

Check and correct the citation at line 135: the RsbU Q317* C-terminal Mn2+ binding site claim is attributed to Ref 25 (Teh et al. 2015), which concerns RsbX phosphatase structure. Supply the correct primary source or restate the claim to match what Ref 25 supports.

Complete the Western blot methods: state whether densitometry was performed and with what software, the normalisation/loading control used, the number of blots quantified, and an explicit fold-over-background threshold defining 'no detectable signal' relative to the pIMK3-only control.
Include Table S1 (and S2) as downloadable supplementary files, and define GSR, ARD, CC, ST and PMSC at first use in the Abstract and Introduction.

Report a quantitative motility metric (halo diameter in mm at a fixed time point, n>=3 independent platings per strain) in a supplementary table and cross-reference it to the LM/IM/HM categories used in Fig. 2B, so the categorical assignment is auditable.

State whether the pIMK3 reporter constructs were sequence-verified before transformation, and specify the NcoI/BamHI insertion sites and selection marker; provide a plasmid map or Addgene/accession reference for pIMK3.

minor_suggestions: Add the explicit signposting sentence at the end of the Introduction stating that the rsbW finding motivates the species-wide start-codon survey, and move the rsbW-to-genome-wide transition to precede the sigB-operon SC section.
State the 1 mM IPTG concentration at first mention in the Fluorescence quantification subsection and confirm in the text that it was used identically for all reporter assays (Figs. 4B and 5C).

Clarify in the text that Hecht et al. 2017 is cited as general precedent for functional non-canonical start codons, and that the ATG>ATA>ATT ranking for rsbW derives entirely from the reporter and immunoblot data in this study.
Add a one-sentence biosafety statement (containment level and institutional approval reference) to Methods.

Specify the acidifying agent used to prepare the pH 2.5 / pH 3.0 BHI, and state which aspects of the acid-challenge and RT-qPCR protocols were adapted from Ref 28 and where they deviate, so a reader need not retrieve that paper to repeat the work.
Give the NCBI accession for the F2365 reference assembly used in the Mauve/BRIG comparisons.
Consider adding catalog numbers (and RRIDs where available) for the anti-GFP primary and anti-rabbit secondary antibodies.
Explain the 500x factor in the 500 x (RFU/OD) fluorescence calculation, and note the plate type and gain setting.
Confirm whether the sigB-null phenotype of MQ140025 was verified experimentally before the evolution experiment began, or state that it was inferred from genotype.

weaknesses.text: The central claim—that altered start codons serve as a regulatory mechanism for fine-tuning SigB activity during adaptation—rests on the assumption that reduced RsbW translation increases SigB activity by perturbing stoichiometry (Figure 4D). However, the manuscript does not directly measure RsbW protein levels or RsbW:SigB ratios in the ARD strains, only infer them from reporter assays in a different genetic background (MQ140025 with pIMK3 plasmid). An alternative explanation is that the non-canonical start codons create a truncated or misfolded RsbW that is non-functional regardless of translation rate; the nonsense mutations in ARD3 and ARD5 (rsbW R23*, Y37*) produce the same SigB hyperactivity phenotype, suggesting loss-of-function rather than stoichiometric tuning. To distinguish these, the authors would need to measure endogenous RsbW protein in ARD strains or show that a synonymous mutation reducing translation rate (without changing the start codon) produces the same effect.

The claim that start codon flexibility in 39 conserved genes represents adaptive selection for niche-specific fitness (lines 395–427) is supported only by phylogenetic association (different codons in different clades) and modest in vitro reporter differences (Figure 5C shows small reduction for GTG vs ATG in plcB and lftR). The manuscript does not demonstrate that these expression differences confer a fitness advantage in any relevant environment, nor does it exclude neutral drift or codon usage bias as alternative explanations for the observed patterns. The statement 'they likely contribute to an overall genomic shift that provides an incremental fitness advantage' (line 426) is speculative and unsupported by the data presented.

Abbreviations and terminology are inconsistent and sometimes undefined at first use: 'GSR' appears in the abstract (line 42) without definition; 'ARD' is used in Figure 1 caption before being defined in text (line 156); 'CC' (clonal complex) and 'ST' (sequence type) are used in the introduction without explicit definition; 'PMSC' (premature stop codon) is introduced at line 208 but the acronym is never expanded in the text. 'SigB-dependent' genes are referenced (e.g., line 186) before the SigB regulon is described.

The narrative structure obscures the central question: the introduction motivates SigB regulation and lists seven genetic targets (line 119) but does not explicitly state that the study will investigate whether translational control of these targets is a regulatory mechanism. The results section presents acid adaptation, then ARD characterization, then genome sequencing, then start codon analysis—a logical experimental sequence but not a logical argument sequence. The reader must infer that the rsbW mutations prompted the genome-wide start codon analysis; this connection is stated only retrospectively at line 248 ('The strong influence of rsbW start codon selection on SigB activity prompted us to investigate...').

Figure 3 is difficult to parse: the circular genome map uses color coding (purple, cyan labels) that is explained only in the caption, and the distinction between mutations in MQ140025 vs. ARDs is not immediately clear from the figure itself. The legend states 'Purple labels denote mutations detected in ARD1, ARD3, and ARD5' but does not explain why these three strains are grouped separately or what the biological significance of their unique mutations is.

The quantitative claim that 'flexible usage of start codons associated with genetic clades in 39 conserved genes' (abstract, line 47) is not precisely defined: does this mean all 39 genes show clade-specific variation, or only some? Table S1 is referenced but not provided in the manuscript, making it impossible to verify the claim or assess the distribution of start codon changes.

Methods section does not specify the IPTG concentration used to induce pIMK3 reporters until line 516 (1 mM), creating ambiguity about whether induction conditions were consistent across all reporter experiments.

The phylogenetic analysis of ST1 strains (Figure S1) is presented as supporting evidence for the evolutionary trajectory of MQ140025 but is not integrated into the main narrative; its relevance to the start codon hypothesis is unclear.

questions: Figure 4D proposes that reduced RsbW translation perturbs RsbW:SigB stoichiometry, but how do you exclude the possibility that non-canonical start codons produce a non-functional RsbW protein (as suggested by the nonsense mutations in ARD3/ARD5 producing identical phenotypes)?
For the 39 genes with flexible start codon usage, what is the distribution of clade-specific variation—do all 39 show the pattern, or is it a subset, and how many strains per clade were analyzed?
Table S1 is cited as containing the complete start codon dataset but is not provided; can this be included or made accessible?
Why were only plcB, lftR, and mntC selected for translational reporter validation among the 13 virulence/stress genes with flexible start codons?

weaknesses.text: The qPCR gene expression comparisons (Figure 2C–G) report fold-changes relative to MQ140025 with statistical significance markers but do not state the test used (paired t-test is mentioned only in the figure legend), do not report exact p-values, and do not apply multiple-comparison correction despite testing six genes across six strains—this is a HARD issue because the family size and correction method are not disclosed, making it impossible to verify whether the reported significances survive correction.

The phylogenetic analysis of ST1 strains (Figure S1, lines 487–494) uses Parsnp2 to infer SNPs associated with branching points but does not report confidence intervals, bootstrap support, or sensitivity to alignment parameters, leaving the evolutionary trajectory claims (lines 354–363) resting on unvalidated tree topology.

Motility assay (Figure 2B) categorizes strains as low, intermediate, or high motility but does not quantify the measurement (halo diameter, time to spread, or other metric) or report n for replicates, making the phenotypic grouping non-reproducible.

The start codon usage analysis (Figure 5, Table S1) identifies 39 genes with flexible usage but does not report confidence intervals or statistical tests for the claim that these genes are enriched in virulence/stress pathways (13 of 39 = 33%) versus the genome background.

Western blot quantification (Figure 4C) shows band intensities but does not state whether densitometry was used, how many replicates were quantified, or whether loading controls were normalized; the figure legend says 'protein samples were collected from three independent experiments' but does not clarify whether all three were quantified.

Acid survival data (Figures 1C–G) plot percentage survival but do not define the error bars (SEM, SD, or CI) or state whether the three independent experiments were averaged before plotting or plotted separately.

The reporter strain fluorescence assay (Figure 4B, 5C) normalizes to OD but does not report the absolute fluorescence values, making it impossible to assess whether the signal-to-noise ratio supports the claimed differences, especially for the ATT construct where 'no detectable signal' is claimed (line 244) without a threshold definition.

questions: What multiple-comparison correction, if any, was applied to the six qPCR gene expression tests in Figure 2, and what are the exact p-values for each comparison?
How were motility phenotypes quantified in Figure 2B, and how many independent replicates were assayed per strain?
Were all three independent Western blot experiments (Figure 4C) quantified by densitometry, and if so, what was the inter-replicate variability?
What defines 'no detectable signal' for the ATT construct in Figure 4B—a fluorescence threshold, a signal-to-noise ratio, or visual inspection of the Western blot?

weaknesses.text: The manuscript does not explicitly state that the work involves only non-pathogenic laboratory manipulation of L. monocytogenes or address biosafety containment level, despite working with a food-borne pathogen; while the work appears to be standard microbiology, a one-sentence biosafety statement would clarify compliance with institutional biosafety committee requirements.

Supplementary data (Tables S1, S2 and Figures S1, S2) are referenced but their availability is not explicitly stated; the authors should confirm whether these are deposited with the preprint or will be made available upon request.

The acknowledgements do not explicitly identify non-author contributions (e.g., Dr. Kate Reddington's role in Nanopore sequencing is thanked but not formally attributed as a contribution), which is a soft transparency issue under current standards.

questions: Does the institution have a biosafety committee approval or statement confirming that this work meets the appropriate biosafety level for L. monocytogenes laboratory culture and genetic manipulation?
Are the supplementary tables and figures (S1, S2) deposited with the preprint or available through a linked repository, or will they be provided upon request?
Were any AI tools or language models used in manuscript preparation, analysis, or figure generation that should be disclosed per emerging authorship guidelines?

weaknesses.text: The manuscript reports (Figure 4B, C) that ATG > ATA > ATT translation efficiency and cites Hecht et al. (2017, ref. 61), but that paper measured initiation rates from all 64 codons in E. coli and reported absolute initiation frequencies, not a direct comparison of ATG vs. ATA vs. ATT in the same genomic context; the manuscript's own reporter data directly demonstrates the hierarchy in L. monocytogenes, which is stronger evidence than the E. coli reference.

The manuscript identifies 39 genes with flexible start codon usage across 60,692 L. monocytogenes genomes and reports that 13 are involved in virulence or stress response, but does not cite prior work systematically documenting start codon polymorphism in Listeria or comparing it to other pathogens, leaving the novelty claim underexamined.

The manuscript proposes that reduced RsbW translation (via non-canonical start codons) or loss of RsbW (via nonsense mutations) increases SigB activity, but does not directly measure RsbW protein levels in the ARD strains to confirm that the stoichiometric perturbation actually occurs; the inference relies on the reporter assay in a heterologous context (pIMK3 plasmid) rather than measurement of endogenous RsbW in the ARD strains themselves.

The manuscript states that GTG SC usage for rsbS might achieve correct stressosome subunit stoichiometry (line 277) but does not cite Listeria-specific experimental evidence that GTG initiation is weaker than ATG; ref. 36 (Cherrak et al. 2024) and ref. 61 (Hecht et al. 2017) provide E. coli data only.

The manuscript does not cite any work on the evolutionary drivers of start codon selection in pathogens under host-specific selective pressure, beyond the Cherrak et al. (2024) example, which is a gap in the discussion of mechanism.

questions: For Figure 4B–C (start codon efficiency): does Hecht et al. (2017) specifically rank ATG, ATA, and ATT in that order, or are you inferring the hierarchy from their broader codon table? If the latter, please clarify that your own reporter data are the primary evidence.

Has flexible start codon usage in Listeria core genes been previously documented in the literature, or is the population-level analysis of 39 genes with variable start codons novel to this work? A brief statement would clarify the novelty.

Do you have quantitative Western-blot measurements of RsbW protein levels in ARD1, ARD6, ARD10, and ARD12 compared to MQ140025, or does the stoichiometric perturbation rest entirely on the reporter assay inference?

weaknesses.text: The central claim—that start codon usage is 'under selection for stress response and virulence genes'—rests on observing that 39 conserved genes show flexible start codon usage and that 13 of these are involved in virulence/stress response. This is a correlation, not evidence of selection. The design does not exclude drift, lineage-specific mutational biases, or structural/codon-usage constraints as explanations for the observed patterns. To establish selection, the authors would need to show that the alternative start codon confers a fitness advantage in the relevant niche, or demonstrate that the pattern is inconsistent with neutral evolution (e.g., via dN/dS analysis or phylogenetic comparative methods). The statement 'these data suggest an evolutionary preference for the usage of specific SC for these genes possibly associated with niche-specific selective pressures' (line 425) is appropriately hedged, but the title and abstract overstate the evidence by claiming start codons are 'under selection' rather than 'show clade-associated variation.'

The reporter assays for plcB and lftR (Figure 5C) show only modest differences in fluorescence between ATG and GTG (described as 'small reduction'), and the manuscript does not establish that this magnitude of difference is biologically meaningful in the context of virulence or stress response. No dose-response relationship is tested, no measurement of endogenous expression levels is provided, and no functional assay (e.g., cell invasion, survival in macrophages) links the altered translation rate to a phenotypic outcome. The claim that 'SC flexibility might provide a genetic means of adjusting gene expression, potentially as a means of enhancing niche specific fitness' (line 302) is speculative without this functional validation.

The design does not rule out the alternative explanation that the rsbW start codon mutations in ARDs are a byproduct of selection for loss-of-function of RsbW itself (via nonsense mutations in ARD3 and ARD5) rather than selection for reduced translation rate. The fact that both nonsense mutations and start codon substitutions occur in the same gene, and both increase SigB activity, suggests that the common target is RsbW inactivation, not fine-tuning of RsbW stoichiometry. The authors argue that 'the primary SC of rsbW accounts for the functional expression under laboratory conditions' (line 248), but this does not exclude the possibility that the start codon mutations are simply a less-efficient route to the same end (loss of RsbW function) that happens to be selected when nonsense mutations are unavailable or deleterious in some genetic background.

questions: Does the phylogenetic distribution of start codon variants in the 39 flexible genes show a pattern inconsistent with neutral drift (e.g., are changes concentrated at recent branching points, or do they predate lineage divergence)?
What is the endogenous expression level of plcB and lftR in strains carrying ATG vs. GTG, and does this correlate with virulence phenotypes in infection models?

For the ARDs, is the fitness cost of hyperactive SigB (reduced growth, smaller colonies) the same for start codon mutants as for nonsense mutants, or does the reduced translation rate confer a selective advantage by partially restoring RsbW function?

The manuscript states that 'the Shine-Dalgarno strength does not correlate closely with translational efficiency' in L. monocytogenes (line 462)—is there evidence that start codon identity, rather than RBS context, is the primary determinant of translation initiation rate in this species?

weaknesses.text: The mechanism by which rsbW start codon mutations increase SigB activity is not experimentally isolated: all ARDs carrying start codon changes simultaneously carry SNPs that alter the first amino acid of RsbV (G111C or G111S), a direct binding partner of RsbW, and no construct separates these dual effects, leaving unclear whether reduced RsbW translation or altered RsbV function is the primary driver.

The evidence for selection on start codon variants is correlational, not causal: phylogenetic clustering is consistent with selection but equally consistent with drift or founder effects, and no fitness assay, environmental condition test, or demonstration that measured translation differences are large enough to be selected for is provided.

The novelty of the core claim is overstated relative to prior work: Hecht et al. (2016) systematically measured translation initiation from all 64 codons and showed non-canonical codons are functional with reduced rates, and Cherrak et al. (2024) explicitly demonstrated that non-canonical start codons confer context-dependent fitness advantages in bacteria; the present manuscript applies this known principle to L. monocytogenes and the SigB system but does not establish a new mechanism.
The GadR R154Q substitution is inferred to impair function based on sequence conservation and low gadT2D2 expression but is not experimentally validated.

The definition of 'flexible' start codon usage as >5% of sequences is arbitrary and not justified; genes with 5–10% variant usage could represent sequencing errors, assembly artifacts, or genuine rare variants, and this distinction is not addressed.

The secondary start codon of rsbW (6 bp downstream) is not tested in the ATA or ATT reporter constructs, leaving ambiguity about whether reduced fluorescence reflects true initiation failure or reinitiation.

The in vitro evolution protocol uses a 1:2500 dilution between acid cycles, which may not accurately mimic gastric passage bottlenecks, and the relevance of selected mutations to natural infection is not established.
The claim that start codon flexibility 'might provide a genetic means of adjusting gene expression' is based on only two genes (plcB, lftR) and is insufficient to support a general principle.

questions: Can the authors provide a construct with the rsbW start codon change (ATG→ATA) but without the RsbV G111C/S substitution to isolate the contribution of each mutation to SigB activation?

For the 39 genes with flexible start codon usage, is there evidence (fitness assay, growth under specific stress, or environmental dependence) that the start codon variants confer a selective advantage, or is the phylogenetic clustering consistent with neutral divergence?

Do the secondary start codons of rsbW (and other genes with flexible start codons) contribute to translation initiation in the ATA and ATT constructs, and if so, how does this affect interpretation of the reporter assay results?

weaknesses.text: **Start codon analysis dataset and code unavailable.** The core contribution—analysis of start codon usage across 60,690 L. monocytogenes genomes—is not reproducible as presented. The authors state they created 'a local blast DNA database for each L. monocytogenes genome sequence' (line 546) and performed custom tblastn searches with specific parameters ('–seg' option enabled, line 547), but provide no code, no deposited database, no intermediate outputs, and no accession numbers for the genome set used. The exact date of NCBI download (24 May 2024, line 546) is noted but the resulting dataset is not archived. Without the processed start codon calls for all 60,690 genomes, the claim that 39 genes show flexible usage (1.8% of 2,180 conserved genes) and that 13 are virulence/stress-related cannot be independently verified. The alternative explanation—that the authors' tblastn parameters or gene-calling thresholds (e.g., the >95% presence threshold for 'conserved' genes, line 554) systematically identified or missed certain genes—cannot be ruled out. This is load-bearing: the entire population-level argument rests on this analysis.

**Phylogenetic analysis of ST1 strains lacks reproducibility details.** The authors inferred phylogeny of 5,546 ST1 genomes using Parsnp2 (line 488) but do not specify the version, alignment parameters, or the exact genome set used (is it the same 60,690 or a subset?). The SNPs associated with branching points (line 492) are examined qualitatively but no tree file, SNP matrix, or reproducible pipeline is provided. Figure S1 and the evolutionary trajectory argument depend on this; without the tree and SNP calls, the claim that GadR R154Q 'occurred much earlier' (line 357) cannot be verified.

**Transcriptional data (qPCR) not deposited.** Gene expression measurements (Figures 2C–G) are presented as fold-changes relative to MQ140025 but raw Ct values, standard deviations, and replicate-level data are not provided in supplementary tables or a data repository. The authors state 'three independent experiments were carried out and each with technical duplicates' (line 857) but do not deposit the underlying qPCR data, making it impossible to verify the statistical tests or reproduce the fold-change calculations.

**Fluorescence and Western blot quantification data not provided.** Figures 4B–C and 5C show quantified results but the underlying pixel intensities, background corrections, and individual replicate measurements are not deposited; the authors note 'three independent experiments were performed' (line 515) but do not provide the raw image files or quantification spreadsheets.

**Strain and plasmid sequences: MQ140025 genome deposited but ARD genomes not.** The complete genome of MQ140025 is available (PRJNA1305691) but the authors sequenced ARD1, 3, 5, 6, 10, and 12 with Illumina reads mapped to MQ140025 (line 485). These reads and the resulting variant calls are not deposited; the authors state 'Purified DNA samples were sent to Novogene' (line 481) but provide no SRA accession or supplementary VCF files, making it impossible to verify the rsbW mutations or check for additional variants.

**Plasmid sequences pLM7UG1 and pLMGC1 not deposited.** The authors identify two plasmids in MQ140025 (lines 206–209) and compare pLMGC1 to Bacillus and Streptococcus plasmids, but do not deposit the MQ140025 plasmid sequences to GenBank or provide them as supplementary FASTA files; only the chromosome is in PRJNA1305691.

**Reporter plasmid construction details incomplete.** The authors state that 'purified recombinant plasmids were electroporated into electrocompetent cells' (line 509) but do not provide the sequences of the three pIMK3-rsbW-eGFP constructs (ATG, ATA, ATT variants) or deposit them in a plasmid repository; verification of the intended mutations and absence of unintended changes is not possible.

**Phylogenetic tree and SNP alignment not provided.** Figure S1 shows a tree of ST1 strains but the Newick file, alignment, or Parsnp2 output is not deposited; the branching points and SNP associations discussed in the Discussion (lines 357–365) cannot be independently inspected.

questions: Where are the processed start codon calls (first three nucleotides) for all 60,690 genomes and the corresponding gene presence/absence matrix deposited, and under what accession?
What is the exact version of Parsnp2 used, and are the core-genome alignment and SNP matrix available?
Are the raw qPCR Ct values, Western blot images, and fluorescence plate reader data (with background corrections) available in a supplementary file or repository?
Are the Illumina sequencing reads and variant calls (VCF) for ARD1, 3, 5, 6, 10, and 12 deposited in the SRA, and if not, why?
Are the sequences of the three pIMK3-rsbW-eGFP constructs (ATG, ATA, ATT) and the pIMK3-plcB and pIMK3-lftR constructs available in a plasmid repository or supplementary file?

weaknesses.text: **Load-bearing claim 1: Start codon flexibility is 'under selection for stress response and virulence genes' (title, abstract, Results section heading).** The evidence is a genome-wide survey showing that 39 conserved genes (1.8% of 2,180) display variable start codons across 60,690 genomes, with 13 of these involved in virulence/stress. However, this is purely correlational: the authors observe that start codon variants cluster by phylogenetic clade (e.g., argB uses ATG in lineage I, GTG in lineage II) but provide no evidence that this clustering reflects selection rather than drift, founder effects, or neutral divergence during lineage splitting. The alternative—that start codon variants arose by chance and were fixed neutrally—is never excluded. The authors note that rsbW non-canonical start codons are 'rare (2 found in 60,690 genomes)' yet claim this supports selection; rarity could equally indicate these are deleterious in most contexts and only beneficial under extreme stress. No phylogenetic comparative method, no dN/dS analysis, no test of whether start codon changes correlate with known selective pressures (e.g., temperature, food vs. clinical niches) is offered. The claim that these variants 'likely contribute to an overall genomic shift that provides an incremental fitness advantage' (line 426) is speculative and unsupported by the data presented.

questions: For the 39 genes with flexible start codons, what is the phylogenetic distribution—do variants cluster by clade, or are they scattered, and does that pattern distinguish selection from drift?

The authors show ATG > ATA > ATT for rsbW but test only plcB and lftR (Fig. 5C) for canonical start codon differences; why not test the other 36 genes claimed to show flexible usage, or at least a representative sample, to establish whether translation efficiency differences are general?

The GadR R154Q mutation in MQ140025 is noted as arising 'much earlier' in the phylogeny (line 357) and associated with a population expansion event; is this a confound for the acid resistance phenotype, and were ARDs tested for GadR status?

Figure 3A shows additional mutations in ARD1, ARD3, and ARD12 beyond rsbW; the authors dismiss these as non-phenotypic, but were these strains re-sequenced to confirm no other rsbW-independent changes arose during the acid challenge?
